name: SkillEvaluator
description: Multi-tier framework for evaluating AI agent skills with quality gates, semantic overlap detection, synthetic evaluation dataset generation, and live agent evaluation that measures how skills affect agent behavior.
readme_content:
# SkillEvaluator ![SkillEvaluator wordmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/ad2815fe78c045db91d230681d32863698da08cf/docs/assets/skillevaluator-wordmark.svg) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-green.svg)](LICENSE) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.12%20%7C%203.13%20%7C%203.14-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/skillevaluator.svg?label=PyPI)](https://pypi.org/project/skillevaluator/) [![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/Documentation-docs.nvidia.com-blue.svg)](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2608.20614-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20614) [![NVIDIA Developer Blog](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blog-NVIDIA%20Developer-76B900.svg)](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/evaluating-ai-agent-skill-performance-with-nvidia-skillevaluator/) > 📺 **Livestream:** [Ask the Experts: Evaluating Agent Skills](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4rI0zATFxYI) SkillEvaluator checks AI agent skills and measures their effect on task results: start with quality checks, then compare runs with and without a skill. Agent skills are folders of instructions and supporting files defined by the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/). SkillEvaluator is part of the [NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline](https://github.com/NVIDIA/skills). ## Get started Three ways in, one CLI, same results.
1. Run the CLI directly 2. Add it to your repo via CI 3. Wire it to your agent
Install (or `uv tool install`): ```bash pip install skillevaluator ``` Run all Tier 1 checks, no API key: ```bash skillevaluator validate \ ./my-skill --tiers 1 ``` Or run from a clone: [Quickstart](#quickstart). Check changed skills on every pull request. On GitHub, run: ```bash skillevaluator ci init ``` It opens a setup PR. On GitLab, copy the [CI template](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/tree/main/ci/bundles/0.9.0). Add the [SkillEvaluator skill](skills/skillevaluator/) to Claude Code, Codex or any skill-aware agent: ```bash npx skills add \ NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator ``` Then ask: *"Is my skill any good?"* No Node.js? [Copy the folder](docs/agent-skill.mdx#install).
Guides: [installation](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/installation), [CI setup](docs/cli-onboarding.mdx) ([GitHub](docs/github-actions.mdx), [GitLab](docs/gitlab-ci.mdx), [report examples](ci/examples/README.md)) and [agent skill](docs/agent-skill.mdx). ## Quickstart Both paths use bundled `text-analyzer`. | Start here | Requires | First result | | --- | --- | --- | | [Run without an LLM](#run-without-an-llm) | Git and uv | A deterministic quality score and findings | | [Use NVIDIA Build](#use-nvidia-build) | Git, uv, and a Build API key | Model-backed rubric scores and feedback | Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) and Git, then get the example: ```bash git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator.git cd SkillEvaluator ``` uv provisions Python 3.13 and dependencies. For standalone installation, see [Installation](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/installation). ### Run without an LLM ```bash uv run --python 3.13 skillevaluator quality-check \ src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer \ -r cli -r json -o reports/first-quality ``` No API key, scanner, GPU or Docker is needed. The example scores **84.5/100 (B)**, exits `0` and saves `reports/first-quality/skillevaluator-quality.json`. The passing threshold defaults to 70. This checks static quality; publication evidence stays `INCOMPLETE`. Security needs scanners; agent impact needs live evaluation. Replace the example path with your skill directory. See the [keyless walkthrough](docs/quickstart.mdx#run-without-an-llm). ### Use NVIDIA Build Eligible NVIDIA Developer Program members can use NVIDIA-hosted endpoints for **free prototyping**, subject to [access terms and rate limits](https://docs.api.nvidia.com/nim/docs/product). 1. Sign in at [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com/) and complete enrollment. 2. Open a model page, select **Get API Key**, and generate your key. 3. Set the provider and key in the same terminal, then run the rubric check: ```bash export SKILL_EVAL_LLM_PROVIDER=nv_build export NVIDIA_API_KEY='nvapi-...' uv run --python 3.13 --extra llm skillevaluator rubric-eval \ src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer \ -r cli -r json -o reports/first-build ``` The command sends skill documentation to the model and saves feedback in `reports/first-build/skillevaluator-rubric.json`. No agent runtime or Docker is needed. Completed evaluations can still fail rubric thresholds. The same key supports Tier 2 embeddings and supported Tier 3 agents. See the [Build walkthrough](docs/quickstart.mdx#use-nvidia-build) or [provider configuration](docs/configuration.mdx). ## Three-tier overview ![SkillEvaluator three-tier pipeline: Skill → Tier 1 Validation → Tier 2 Deduplication → Tier 3 Live Evaluation → Reports](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/ad2815fe78c045db91d230681d32863698da08cf/docs/assets/three-tier-overview.svg) Each tier is independent. Add its extra to your command: | Tier | Question | Example after setup | Additional setup | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Tier 1: Validation | Is the skill safe, well-formed and [harness-compatible](docs/tier1-validation.mdx#the-checks)? | `uv run skillevaluator tier1 ./my-skill --no-llm` | External scanners for full static coverage; a provider and model clients enable LLM checks | | Tier 2: Deduplication | Does guidance repeat or overlap? | `uv run --extra tier2 skillevaluator tier2 ./my-skill` | Embeddings and chat; add `--catalog ./skill-catalog.json` for inter-skill comparison | | Tier 3: Live Evaluation | Does the skill help the agent? | `uv run --extra tier3 skillevaluator tier3 ./my-skill` | Provider access, a supported agent, and a running sandbox (Docker by default) | Tier 1 fetches pinned, verified SkillSpector and Gitleaks releases when they are missing; Semgrep is optional. See [scanners](docs/installation.mdx#system-tools). `--no-llm` does not remove scanner requirements; a scanner that cannot run is `INCOMPLETE` and exits nonzero. [SkillSpector](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillSpector) provides specialized skill security scanning; [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor), the open-source agent evaluation framework, powers sandboxed agent runs. Tier 2 reports when inter-skill comparison did not run. Tier 3 autopilot reuses sources or creates one skill-grounded case with limited coverage. See [tier guides](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/). ## Run the combined pipeline After setting up the provider, scanners, and agent sandbox, run all three tiers: ```bash uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator doctor --env-mode docker uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator validate ./my-skill ``` `doctor` checks readiness, not inference success. `validate` runs all tiers with autopilot for skills. Use `--tiers 1,2` to skip live evaluation or `--tiers 1` for static checks. `--no-autopilot` requires an existing source. Other artifact types retain their applicable stages. Tier 1 gates `validate`. Tier 2 gates unless `--no-block-on-dedup` is set; Tier 3 gates only with `--block-on-agent-eval`. Model and managed-sandbox usage can incur charges; see [runtime and cost](docs/tier3-live-evaluation.mdx#plan-for-cost). Standalone generation needs substantive `evals/EVAL.md` guidance, a `--prompt` file with task requests and outcomes, or matching retained traces. `--force` below replaces the autopilot starter; `--refine` refines it. Explicit `--grounding skill` permits skill-only starters. Review cases; templates omit unauthored negatives. ```bash uv run --python 3.13 --extra tier3 skillevaluator tier3 create-eval-dataset ./my-skill --full --prompt eval-guidance.md --force ``` ## Run from a source checkout Use `uv run --python 3.13` with the relevant extra. See [Installation](docs/installation.mdx#choosing-extras) for extras and standalone upgrades. ## Research and citation Resources: [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20614), [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.20614), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.20614), [BibTeX](https://arxiv.org/bibtex/2608.20614), and the [NVIDIA Developer blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/evaluating-ai-agent-skill-performance-with-nvidia-skillevaluator/). Cite the paper and record the SkillEvaluator release or commit; see [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff). ## Documentation See [the documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/) for setup, tier guides, reports, CI integration, CLI reference, and [performance dashboard](docs/reports.mdx#performance-dashboard). ## Installation and third-party software Follow the [installation guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/installation) to choose the full installation or a smaller per-tier setup. This project will download and install additional third-party open source software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before use. ## Contributing Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and run: ```bash make lint && make test && make build ``` See [project governance](GOVERNANCE.md) and the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). ## Support Support level: **Experimental**. Community-supported, best-effort, with no SLA or NVIDIA enterprise support entitlement. Report bugs and feature requests through [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/issues); see [SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md). ## Security Report suspected vulnerabilities using the private process in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Do not disclose security issues in a public GitHub issue. ## Releases Release changes are recorded in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) and [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/releases). ## License Apache License 2.0 — see [LICENSE](LICENSE), [NOTICE](NOTICE), and [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.

# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

[build-system]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"
requires = ["setuptools >= 77", "wheel"]

[project]
name = "skillevaluator"
version = "0.9.0"
description = "Multi-tier framework for evaluating AI agent skills with quality gates, semantic overlap detection, synthetic evaluation dataset generation, and live agent evaluation."
authors = [{ name = "NVIDIA Corporation" }]
readme = "README.md"
keywords = [
    "skills-evaluation",
    "skills",
    "skill-uplift",
    "ai-agents",
    "security",
    "vulnerability-scanner",
    "claude-code",
]
classifiers = [
    "Environment :: Console",
    "Operating System :: OS Independent",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.12",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.13",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.14",
    "Topic :: Software Development :: Quality Assurance",
]
requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.15"
license = "Apache-2.0"
license-files = [
    "LICENSE",
    "NOTICE",
    "THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md",
]
# Base install is static-validation capable (Tier 1) and must NOT pull Harbor
# or LLM clients. Those live behind the extras below.
dependencies = [
    # Tier 1 Code Risk Analysis scanner, which validate runs by default.
    "bandit>=1.9.4",
    "click>=8.3.3,<9",
    "idna>=3.10,<4",
    "jinja2>=3.1",
    "markdown-it-py>=4.2,<5",
    "packaging>=24",
    "pydantic>=2.11.0",
    "pyyaml>=6.0",
    # Dataset-authored signal patterns require a per-match timeout.
    "regex>=2024.11.6",
    "rich>=13.5.0",
    # Runs the pinned SkillSpector wheel in its own environment (uv tool run),
    # so a plain pip install can complete the Tier 1 security check.
    "uv>=0.11.27",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
# Shared public LLM / embedding clients used by LLM-backed checks, Tier 2, and Tier 3.
llm = [
    "anthropic>=0.83.0",
    "boto3>=1.34.0",
    "litellm>=1.92.0,<1.94.0.dev0",
    "openai>=2.21.0",
]
# Tier 2 intra-skill deduplication and local-catalog inter-skill similarity.
tier2 = [
    "skillevaluator[llm]",
]
# Tier 3 live agent evaluation through Harbor's native environments.
tier3 = [
    "skillevaluator[llm]",
    "harbor[gke]==0.25.0",
    # CVE-2026-59950, CVE-2026-52870, and CVE-2026-52869 fixed floor.
    "mcp>=1.28.1,<2",
    # CVE-2026-48522 through CVE-2026-48526 fixed floor.
    "pyjwt[crypto]>=2.13.0",
    # GHSA-hj66-6f7g-4r5v and GHSA-xpv3-w29h-x7cv fixed floor (via harbor[gke]).
    "oauthlib>=4.0.0",
    # PYTHON_DOTENV_DISABLED, which keeps Harbor from loading .env files, needs 1.2.0.
    "python-dotenv>=1.2.0",
]
# Scanner for the opt-in Dependency Vulnerability Audit (`--check dependency`).
security = [
    "pip-audit>=2.10.0",
]
# Verify GitHub-signed execution receipts for the optional CI report publisher.
publisher = [
    "pyjwt[crypto]>=2.13.0",
]
# Optional local UI for comparing saved reports; never imported by base commands.
dashboard = [
    # server.allowedHosts, which limits the dashboard to loopback host names, needs 1.61.
    "streamlit>=1.61,<2",
]
# Full public install convenience bundle.
all = [
    "skillevaluator[tier2,tier3,security]",
]
dev = [
    "skillevaluator[publisher]",
    # PyPA build backs the `make build` target.
    "build>=1.2",
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "pytest>=8.4.0",
    "pytest-cov>=6.2.0",
    # pytest-xdist carried over for parallel test execution (-n auto).
    "pytest-xdist>=3.6.0",
    # Ruff 0.16 enables new rules that require a dedicated repository-wide cleanup.
    "ruff>=0.15.4,<0.16",
]

[project.urls]
Documentation = "https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator#readme"
Repository = "https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator"

[project.scripts]
# Single console script for the consolidated distribution.
skillevaluator = "skillevaluator.cli:cli"

[tool.uv]
managed = true

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]
include = ["skillevaluator*"]

[tool.setuptools.package-data]
"skillevaluator.tier3" = ["grader_reference/*.json", "grader_reference/trajectories/*.json"]
"skillevaluator" = ["ci-release.json", "ci-release-all-tiers.json"]
"skillevaluator.config" = ["*.yaml", "profiles/*.yaml"]
"skillevaluator.harness" = ["profiles/*.yaml"]
"skillevaluator.reporting" = ["templates/*.j2", "assets/*.js", "assets/*.md"]
"skillevaluator.tier3.harbor" = [
    "templates/*.py",
    "templates/*.sh",
]
"skillevaluator.tier3.reference_skills" = [
    "*/SKILL.md",
    "*/evals/*.json",
    "*/evals/*.jsonl",
    "*/evals/*.yaml",
    "*/evals/*.yml",
    "*/evals/harbor/**/*",
    "*/evals/files/**/*",
    "*/references/**/*",
    "*/scripts/*.py",
    "*/scripts/*.sh",
    "*/files/**/*",
    "*/environment/docker-compose*.yml",
    "*/environment/docker-compose*.yaml",
    "*/mcp_servers.toml",
]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 120
target-version = "py312"
src = ["src", "tests"]
exclude = ["**/evals/results/**", ".venv", "build", "dist"]

name: claude-plugins-official
description: Official, Anthropic-managed directory of high quality Claude Code Plugins.
readme_content:
# Claude Plugins

Anthropic's own plugins for Claude, and the `claude-plugins-official` marketplace for Claude Code.

> **Submitting a plugin?** Submit it at **[claude.ai/directory/manage](https://claude.ai/directory/manage)**. Plugins accepted there are served across Claude products. Pull requests to this repository are not monitored.

## What is changing

- **All plugins are now submitted at [claude.ai/directory/manage](https://claude.ai/directory/manage)**, and are served across Claude products from there.
- **`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` is being phased out for third-party plugins.** It will be reduced over time to Anthropic's own plugins.
- **This repository is the home of Anthropic's own plugins.** Its checks cover the plugin folders here, not the plugins hosted in other repositories.

> **⚠️ Important:** Make sure you trust a plugin before installing, updating, or using it. Anthropic does not control what MCP servers, files, or other software are included in plugins and cannot verify that they will work as intended or that they won't change. See each plugin's homepage for more information.

## Structure

- **`/plugins`** - Internal plugins developed and maintained by Anthropic
- **`/external_plugins`** - Third-party plugins added before submissions moved to [claude.ai/directory/manage](https://claude.ai/directory/manage), and Anthropic's channel plugins (Discord, fakechat, iMessage and Telegram)

## Installation

Plugins can be installed directly from this marketplace via Claude Code's plugin system.

To install, run `/plugin install {plugin-name}@claude-plugins-official`

or browse for the plugin in `/plugin > Discover`

## Contributing

### Third-party plugins

Submit and manage your plugin at [claude.ai/directory/manage](https://claude.ai/directory/manage). Do not open a pull request here: pull requests are not monitored, and `marketplace.json` is being reduced to Anthropic's own plugins.

### Anthropic plugins

Plugins in `/plugins` are developed by Anthropic team members. See `/plugins/example-plugin` for a reference implementation. Every folder there is checked on each pull request, whether or not `marketplace.json` lists it.

## Plugin Structure

Each plugin follows a standard structure:

```
plugin-name/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json      # Plugin metadata (required)
├── .mcp.json            # MCP server configuration (optional)
├── commands/            # Slash commands (optional)
├── agents/              # Agent definitions (optional)
├── skills/              # Skill definitions (optional)
└── README.md            # Documentation
```

## Plugin names are immutable

The `name` field in a marketplace entry is an **immutable slug**. Once a plugin has been published, its `name` must not change — users have it installed under that slug, and renaming it breaks their install with a `plugin-not-found` error.

- To change how a plugin is labeled in the UI, set or update `displayName` instead.
- If a rename is genuinely unavoidable, add an entry to the top-level `renames` map in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` so existing installs auto-migrate:

```json
"renames": {
  "old-name": "new-name"
}
```

The Claude Code plugin loader reads this map and transparently rewrites the old slug to the new one on the user's next sync.

## Skill-bundle plugins

When a plugin's source repository ships skills (`SKILL.md` files) without a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, the marketplace entry can declare the skills directly using `strict: false` and an explicit `skills` array.

```json
{
  "name": "example-bundle",
  "description": "Brief description of the bundled skills.",
  "author": { "name": "Author Name" },
  "category": "development",
  "source": {
    "source": "git-subdir",
    "url": "https://github.com/example-org/sdk.git",
    "path": "packages/agent-skills",
    "ref": "main",
    "sha": "<commit sha>"
  },
  "strict": false,
  "skills": [
    "./skill-a",
    "./skill-b",
    "./skill-c"
  ],
  "homepage": "https://github.com/example-org/sdk"
}
```

Each path in `skills` is relative to `source.path` and points at a directory containing a `SKILL.md`. Paths can reach deeper than a single level — for example, `["./libA/skill-1", "./libB/skill-2"]` exposes a curated subset across multiple library subdirectories. Each skill is registered as `<plugin-name>:<skill-name>` in Claude Code.

For the underlying schema, see [Strict mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-marketplaces) in the marketplace documentation.

## License

Please see each linked plugin for the relevant LICENSE file.

## Documentation

For more information on developing Claude Code plugins, see the [official documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins).

name: LibreTranslate
description: Free and Open Source Machine Translation API. Self-hosted, offline capable and easy to setup.
readme_content:
# LibreTranslate

[Try it online!](https://libretranslate.com) | [API Docs](https://docs.libretranslate.com) | [Community Forum](https://community.libretranslate.com/) | [Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/libretranslate.com)

[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/libretranslate)](https://pypi.org/project/libretranslate) [![Run tests](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/workflows/Run%20tests/badge.svg)](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/actions?query=workflow%3A%22Run+tests%22) [![Build and Publish Docker Image](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/actions/workflows/publish-docker.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/actions/workflows/publish-docker.yml) [![Publish package](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/actions/workflows/publish-package.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/actions/workflows/publish-package.yml) [![Awesome Humane Tech](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/humanetech-community/awesome-humane-tech/main/humane-tech-badge.svg?sanitize=true)](https://codeberg.org/teaserbot-labs/delightful-humane-design)

Free and Open Source Machine Translation API, entirely self-hosted. Unlike other APIs, it doesn't rely on proprietary software such as Google or Azure to perform translations. Instead, its translation engine is powered by the open source [Argos Translate](https://github.com/argosopentech/argos-translate) library.

![Translation](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/457696b5-dbff-40ab-a18e-7bfb152c5121)

## Getting Started

- [Quickstart](https://docs.libretranslate.com/)
- [Usage Instructions](https://docs.libretranslate.com/guides/api_usage/)
- [Community Resources](https://docs.libretranslate.com/community/resources/)

## Credits

This work is largely possible thanks to [Argos Translate](https://github.com/argosopentech/argos-translate), which powers the translation engine.

## License

[GNU Affero General Public License v3](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html)

## Trademark

See [Trademark Guidelines](https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/blob/main/TRADEMARK.md)

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]

[project]

name = "libretranslate"

license = { file = "LICENSE" }
authors = [

    { name = "LibreTranslate Authors" },
]

keywords = [

]
dynamic = ["version"]

dependencies = [

    "Flask-Limiter ==2.6.3",
    "Flask-Babel ==3.1.0",
    "waitress ==2.1.2",
    "expiringdict ==1.2.2",
    "langdetect==1.0.9",
    "lexilang==1.0.7",
    "minisbd==0.9.5",
    "APScheduler ==3.11.2",
    "argos-translate-files ==1.4.4",
    "itsdangerous ==2.1.2",
    "Werkzeug ==2.3.8",
    "requests ==2.31.0",
    "redis ==4.4.4",
    "numpy <2;python_version<='3.12'",
    "numpy ==2.3.5;python_version>='3.13'",
    "prometheus-client ==0.15.0",
    "polib ==1.1.1",
    "packaging ==23.1",
]

[project.scripts]
libretranslate = "libretranslate.main:main"
ltmanage = "libretranslate.manage:manage"


[project.optional-dependencies]
test = [
    "pytest >=7.2.0",
    "pytest-cov",
    "pre-commit >=3.0.0",
    "types-requests",
    "pip-audit"
]


[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://libretranslate.com"
Source = "https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate"
Documentation = "https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate"
Tracker = "https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/issues"
History = "https://github.com/LibreTranslate/LibreTranslate/releases"

[tool.hatch.build]
artifacts = ["*.mo"]

[tool.hatch.metadata]
allow-direct-references = true

# ENVIRONMENTS AND SCRIPTS
[tool.hatch.envs.default]
features = [
    "test",
]
post-install-commands = [
    "pre-commit install",
]


[tool.hatch.envs.default.scripts]
dev = "python main.py {args}"
locales = "python scripts/compile_locales.py"
fmt = [
    "pre-commit run --all --all-files",
]
test = [
    "fmt",
    "pytest {args}",
]
cov = [
    "pytest --cov-report html {args}",
    "python -c 'import webbrowser; webbrowser.open(\"http://0.0.0.0:3000\")'",
    "python -m http.server 3000 --directory ./htmlcov",
]


[[tool.hatch.envs.all.matrix]]
python = ["3.8", "3.9", "3.10", "3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]


# TOOLS
[tool.hatch.version]
path = "VERSION"
pattern = "^(?P<version>[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*)$"


[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = [
    "-v",
    "--cov=libretranslate",
    "--color=yes",
    "--cov-report=term-missing",
]

ignore = [
    "E501", # line too long
    "A003", # Class attribute is shadowing a python builtin
    "S101", # Use of `assert` detected
    "S311", # Standard pseudo-random generators are not suitable for cryptographic purposes
    "T201", "T203", # remove print and pprint
    "E402", # Module level import not at top of file
]

name: Claude-BugHunter
description: A Claude Code skill bundle for bug hunting and external red-team work - 82 skills, 15 slash commands, 681 disclosed-report patterns curated across 24 core vulnerability classes, plus enterprise identity + infrastructure attack matrices.
readme_content:
![claude-bughunter banner](assets/banner-v2.svg) # claude-bughunter > A self-contained Claude skill bundle for bug hunting and external red-team work · **83 skills** · 15 slash commands · **681 disclosed-report patterns** (433 now individually cited & auditable) across 24 core vulnerability classes · enterprise identity + infrastructure attack matrices · engagement-folder scaffolding · Burp MCP integration · battle-tested across authorized red-team and bug-hunting engagements, plus public training platforms (DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Hacker101, testphp.vulnweb.com). Built by **[Sachin Sharma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sachinsharma8080/)** — Bug Hunting & GenAI Security Research.

SPONSORED BY
    

--- ## What is this? `claude-bughunter` is a drop-in skill bundle for the [Claude Code skills system](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills). Install once and Claude Code stops being a chatbot and starts behaving like a senior bug-hunting researcher or red-team operator: it knows the techniques, the chain templates, the VRT mappings, the platform CVE chains, and the hygiene — and it stays in scope. Four layers stack: - **Think** — `bb-methodology` + `redteam-mindset`: the 5-phase non-linear workflow, critical-thinking framework, and red-team operator discipline. - **Hunt webapps** — 58 `hunt-*` skills curated from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports: per-class detection patterns, payloads, bypass tables, and chain templates. - **Hit the perimeter** — enterprise platform chains (M365/Entra, Okta, vCenter, SSL-VPN appliances, SharePoint, cloud IAM): current 2024–2026 CVE chains + post-credential escalation. - **Ship it** — `triage-validation` + reporting + `evidence-hygiene`: the 7-Question Gate, VRT-aware severity, OOS rebuttals, PII redaction, and red-team deliverables. All triggered automatically by topic — describe what you're testing in plain English and the relevant skill loads. No invocation by name. --- ## Quickstart **Option A — install as a Claude Code plugin (recommended).** From inside Claude Code: ```text /plugin marketplace add elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter /plugin install claude-bughunter@elementalsouls ``` All 83 skills + 15 commands load namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` and update when you bump the plugin version — no files copied into `~/.claude/`. **Option B — copy install (no plugin system / pin to a clone):** ```bash git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git cd Claude-BugHunter ``` ```bash # macOS / Linux bash scripts/install.sh # Windows (PowerShell) pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1 ``` Both copy the skills + commands into `~/.claude/` (macOS/Linux) or `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\` (Windows) and wire the `hunt` engagement scaffolder. **What each install path gives you:** | Path | 83 skills + 15 slash commands | `cbh` CLI | `hunt` scaffolder | |---|---|---|---| | **A — plugin** | ✅ namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` | ➕ separate `pipx install` | ❌ clone-only | | **B — copy install** | ✅ copied into `~/.claude/` | ✅ from the clone | ✅ from the clone | The plugin is the fastest path to the skills + slash commands. The terminal-native `cbh` runner installs standalone — `pipx install git+https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter` — so plugin users can add it without a full clone (see [`cbh` CLI](docs/cbh-cli.md)). The `hunt` engagement scaffolder ships with the clone (Option B). That's it. Open Claude Code and describe what you're testing in plain English — the right skill loads automatically, no invocation by name: ```text > Testing acme.com — an in-scope HackerOne target. Run recon and rank the surface. ⟳ loading skills: web2-recon, offensive-osint, bb-methodology … → subdomain enum (subfinder + crt.sh) … 47 hosts → live hosts (httpx) … 12 · tech fingerprint … 6 distinct stacks → ranked surface: api.acme.com (GraphQL, introspection ON) ← start here auth.acme.com (OAuth, SSO) ← hunt-oauth Next: want me to probe the GraphQL introspection + OAuth redirect_uri? ``` → Full [Installation guide](INSTALL.md) · [Usage guide](USAGE.md) · [searchable skill catalog](docs/skills.md). > The block above is an illustrative transcript. To record a real demo of your own session: `asciinema rec demo.cast` → upload to [asciinema.org](https://asciinema.org) and drop the badge here. --- ## Runs on multiple agent harnesses ![One install, agent harnesses — Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Google AntiGravity](assets/harness-routing.svg) The skills are plain [Agent Skills](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills) — the same `SKILL.md` format that **Claude Code · OpenCode · OpenAI Codex CLI · Hermes Agent · Google AntiGravity** all load. One command installs them everywhere: ```bash # macOS / Linux bash scripts/install.sh --all --burp-mcp # Windows (PowerShell) pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1 -All -BurpMcp ``` | Harness | Target Skill Directory | Flag | |---|---|---| | **Claude Code** (baseline) | `~/.claude/skills/` | *(default)* | | **OpenCode** | reads `~/.claude/skills/` & `~/.agents/skills/` | *(default)* / `--agents` | | **OpenAI Codex CLI** | `~/.agents/skills/` | `--agents` | | **Hermes Agent** | `~/.hermes/skills/` | `--hermes` | | **Google AntiGravity** | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` | `--antigravity` | `--all` (`-All`) detects installed harnesses and copies skills to each harness's path (`~/.claude/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.hermes/skills`, `~/.gemini/config/skills`); `--burp-mcp` (`-BurpMcp`) wires the Burp MCP server into each. The full *knowledge* layer ports to all five — the slash commands and `/hunt` engine stay Claude-Code-only by design. → [Multi-harness guide](docs/multi-harness.md) --- ## Star History Chart is self-hosted — regenerate with `python3 scripts/gen_star_history.py` (needs `gh auth login`). Refreshes automatically each day via `.github/workflows/star-history.yml`. --- ## Scope — what this bundle is for, and what it isn't This bundle covers the **external attack surface** — anything reachable from the internet without first compromising an internal endpoint. ### In scope - **Bug bounty hunting** — web apps, APIs, SaaS, GraphQL, OAuth, JWT, file upload, IDOR, SSRF, RCE chains - **Web application pentesting** — full hunt-* coverage of OWASP-mapped bug classes + discipline rules - **External red-team engagements** — initial-access against internet-facing enterprise estate: M365 / Entra ID, Okta-as-IdP, SharePoint on-prem (ToolShell + legacy SOAP), VMware vCenter / Workspace ONE, SSL VPN appliances (Cisco / Fortinet / Citrix / Palo Alto / Pulse / SonicWall / F5), Android APK red-team, supply-chain recon - **Cloud misconfig + post-credential escalation** — public S3, IMDS chains, STS AssumeRole, cross-account confused-deputy - **Recon + OSINT** — subdomain enum, identity-fabric mapping, certificate transparency, JS analysis, secret scanning - **Reporting** — H1, Bugcrowd (VRT-aware), Intigriti, Immunefi, plus client-facing red-team deliverable format ### Out of scope (deliberate — not gaps, design decisions) - **Internal Active Directory attacks** — BloodHound, Kerberoasting, ASREProast, DCSync, Pass-the-Hash, AD CS abuse, ntlmrelayx, Responder, PetitPotam, etc. Different operational risk profile; needs different tooling and judgment. **Future bundle, not this one.** - **C2 frameworks** — Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, BRC4 tradecraft. Out of scope for external-only engagement model. - **Post-exploit / persistence / lateral** — Mimikatz/comsvcs LSASS dumping, golden/silver tickets, named-pipe impersonation, persistence (registry, scheduled tasks, WMI events, COM hijacking), token theft. These start after the perimeter has already broken — different bundle territory. - **Evasion** — AMSI bypass, ETW patching, AV/EDR bypass. Tied to C2 tradecraft above. - **iOS pentesting / hardware / RF / ICS** — out of scope by design. - **Binary exploitation / kernel pwn / browser internals** — different skill universe. If you're running an internal red team that includes domain-takeover chains via Kerberos or lateral movement, **this bundle won't help you in those phases** — and we'd rather say that up front than have you find out mid-engagement. The external surface handoff to internal-RT tooling (Impacket, NetExec, CrackMapExec, Rubeus, Certify, BloodHound) is intentionally outside our scope. **Coverage for internal AD and post-exploit may come in a future update.** --- ## What's inside **83 skills**, auto-loaded by topic — no invocation by name. Coverage across the external attack surface: | Category | # | Examples | |---|---|---| | Hunt — web app vuln classes | 58 | XSS, SQLi, SSRF, IDOR, LFI, SSTI, XXE, CSRF, CORS, open-redirect, SharePoint, ASP.NET/NTLM | | Enterprise platform attack ★ | 10 | M365/Entra, Okta, cloud-IAM-deep, vCenter, enterprise VPN, APK/iOS red-team pipelines, supply-chain recon | | Reporting & validation | 6 | triage-validation, evidence-hygiene, report-writing, bugcrowd-reporting | | Recon & OSINT | 5 | web2-recon, offensive-osint, osint-methodology, recon-scope-triage | | Methodology & mindset | 4 | bb-methodology, bug-bounty, redteam-mindset, bb-local-toolkit | Full searchable catalog → **[docs/skills.md](docs/skills.md)**. Also ships **15 slash commands** (`/hunt`, `/recon`, `/report`, …) and a deterministic **engagement engine** (`engine/`) that maps a target's attack surface and routes each finding to the skill that handles it. --- ## How it works A 6-phase, non-linear workflow — **recon → map & rank → hunt → validate → report** — with scope enforced in code and a **7-Question Gate** before anything is submitted. Two ways to drive it: - **Plain English** — describe what you're testing and the relevant skill loads automatically. - **`/hunt` scaffold + `cbh` CLI** — engagement-folder structure, state, and orchestration. → [Usage guide & worked example](USAGE.md) · [6-phase architecture & skill-to-phase map](docs/architecture.md) · [`cbh` CLI](docs/cbh-cli.md) --- ## Authorization These skills are intended for assets you **own** or have **written authorization to assess** (bug-bounty in-scope assets, pentest engagement letters, CTF challenges, your own infrastructure). The skills include validation gates that auto-trigger when you point Claude at unverified third-party targets — `triage-validation`'s 7-Question Gate explicitly asks whether the asset is in scope (Q3) and on the program's accepted-impact list (Q2). The `bugcrowd-reporting` skill includes researcher-side hygiene (Bugcrowdninja alias, account-state restoration, friendly-tester posture) that signals legitimate authorized testing to the target's fraud team. The bundle explicitly **excludes**: weaponizing 0-days against unauthorized targets, post-exploitation tooling, malware development, mass-targeting infrastructure. See [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) for the full posture. > **Heads-up — Anthropic runtime cyber safeguards.** Anthropic's models apply real-time

[Try Qwen Code 1.0 Preview](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/tree/v1.0.0-preview) · [Documentation](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/1.x/) · [中文文档](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/1.x/zh/users/overview/). | ## Why Qwen Code? - **Agentic out of the box** — Auto-Memory, Skills, SubAgents, and MCP work from the first session. Agent Teams, Agent Arena, and Dynamic Workflows are built in too — experimental or opt-in, as noted in [Capabilities](#capabilities). - **Open-source, inside and out** — The framework and the Qwen models are open-source. They evolve together. No vendor lock-in. - **Multi-protocol** — Supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Qwen APIs. Any third-party provider or local model (Ollama / vLLM). Switch at runtime. - **Beyond the terminal** — IDE plugins, Desktop app, Web UI, SDKs, and chat integrations (Telegram / DingTalk / WeChat / WeCom / Feishu and more). > [!TIP] > Qwen Code is actively iterating on itself — using its own agent and models to file issues, submit PRs, review code, and run tests. Powered by the community, driven by AI. ## Installation Looking for **Qwen Code 1.0 Preview**? [Get started here](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/tree/v1.0.0-preview). The instructions below are for the main version. **Linux / macOS:** ```bash curl -fsSL https://qwen-code-assets.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/installation/install-qwen-standalone.sh | bash ``` **Windows:** ```powershell irm https://qwen-code-assets.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/installation/install-qwen-standalone.ps1 | iex ``` > Restart your terminal after installation to ensure environment variables take effect.
NPM / Homebrew **NPM** (requires [Node.js 22+](https://nodejs.org/)): ```bash npm install -g @qwen-code/qwen-code@latest ``` **Homebrew** (macOS / Linux): ```bash brew install qwen-code ```
## Quick Start Open a terminal in your project and start Qwen Code: ```bash cd /path/to/your-project qwen ``` Inside the session, run `/auth` and choose [**Qwen Account with Subscription**](https://chat.qwen.ai/?memberPlan=qwen_code&entry=qwen_code&paywallScene=cli) to sign in with your **Plus or Pro subscription**, or configure a provider with an API key. Then try: ```text Explain this repository and show me where to start. ``` See the [Authentication Guide](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/configuration/auth/) and [Settings Reference](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/configuration/settings/) for detailed setup.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- macOS, Windows, and Linux. | | **Web** | Run `qwen serve --open` to open the [Web UI](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/qwen-serve/) in your browser. _(experimental)_ | | **Editor** | Set up [VS Code](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/integration-vscode/), [Zed](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/integration-zed/), or [JetBrains](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/integration-jetbrains/). | | **Chat** | Connect [Telegram](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/features/channels/telegram/), [DingTalk](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/features/channels/dingtalk/), [WeChat](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/features/channels/weixin/), [GitHub](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/features/channels/github/), then run `qwen channel start`. See the [Channels overview](https://qwenlm.github.io/qwen-code-docs/en/users/features/channels/overview/) for webhook senders and plugin adapters. | For automation and custom integrations: - **Headless** — Run `qwen -p "..."` in scripts, CI/CD, or batch jobs. - **SDKs** — Build with [TypeScript](./packages/sdk-typescript/README.md), [Python](./packages/sdk-python/README.md), or [Java](./packages/sdk-java/qwencode/README.md). - **Daemon** — Run `qwen serve` to connect clients over HTTP + SSE (ACP). _(experimental)_ [

name: LoopForge
description: Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.
readme_content:
English · 简体中文

Two ways to work · Quick start · SOPs · Features · Local · FAQ · Docs

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8af401d9-1aae-427c-b4bc-455c12d17beb

80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an **SOP** (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in. Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license. ## Two ways to work | | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run an SOP** | | --- | --- | --- | | Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off | | How it runs | Main Bot opens a [conversation workspace](docs/conversation-workspaces.md) (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents | The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-SOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox | | You stay in control by | Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running SOP from chat | Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node | | Delivers | A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (`mode=direct`) | Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs | Both paths track the same **requirements**, so every change, whether made in chat or by an SOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, SOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.

## Why LoopForge Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships. - **Repeatable.** Same SOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product SOPs. - **Separated roles.** Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as an SOP node or as a subagent in chat. - **Human in the loop.** Approval gates where they matter. Read the report, approve, or send the work back to a chosen step. - **Observable and resumable.** Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node. - **Your stack, your servers.** Ten coding-agent CLIs as executors, from CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code to OpenCode, Cursor CLI and more. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime. ## Quick start Install **Git** and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set `LOOPFORGE_YES=1` to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git cd LoopForge ./start.sh ``` `./start.sh` pulls the GHCR release image pinned in `compose.yaml` without building locally (`bash scripts/install.sh` does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter SOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use `./start.sh logs`, `stop`, `restart` or `pull` to manage it, and `./start.sh dev` to build the checkout from source. If downloads from `ghcr.io` stall, set `MIRROR` to a registry host that can stand in for `ghcr.io`. `./start.sh` pulls from that host and tags the image back to the name pinned in `compose.yaml`. Setting `MIRROR` trusts that host, because the download is tagged with the official name. The GitHub Release records the digest; `docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:` should show the same digest after `@`. Without `MIRROR`, `./start.sh` still pulls `ghcr.io` directly, and `compose.yaml` stays unchanged. Upgrade with the same variable and `./start.sh pull`. [ghcr.nju.edu.cn](https://doc.nju.edu.cn/books/e1654/page/ghcr) is one such host. A Docker `registry-mirrors` entry such as `https://docker.nju.edu.cn` only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for `MIRROR`. ```bash MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh ``` Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on `0.0.0.0:8090` by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing an SOP. For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, [set up Git SSH](docs/deployment.md#git-repositories-over-ssh) to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP. ### Try it without an API key New accounts join the **LoopForge demo project**, which includes an SOP made only of a script and a human gate: 1. Switch to the demo project, open **Templates**, and open **Platform check · script & approval**. 2. Click **Run SOP**. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step. 3. Approve it from **Needs review** or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact. ### What you need for real work | I want to… | You need | | --- | --- | | Run the script + approval demo | Nothing | | Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project | An API key for the selected executor | | Change an existing repository (in chat or via an SOP) and open a PR | Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings) |
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model
- **Executors.** Pick one of ten CLIs beside the home composer, then a model. Every SOP role can choose its executor independently (built-in roles default to CodeBuddy). Requirement clarification, AI notification summaries, Bot replies and run evals currently use CodeBuddy, so their model pickers list CodeBuddy models only and the server refuses a model of another CLI instead of switching it to CodeBuddy; scheduled assistant tasks run on the CLI the task selects. | Executor | Credentials | Installation | | --- | --- | --- | | **CodeBuddy** | Personal key, or a shared key an administrator configures for chat and SOP runs | In the Docker image | | **Codex** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | In the Docker image | | **Claude Code** | Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **OpenCode · Kimi Code · Pi** | Personal key only | Installed from npm on first use, then cached | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Personal key only | In the Docker image | | **Cursor CLI · Antigravity** | Personal key only | Provider installer on first chat use; not installed into SOP sandboxes | | **ZCode** | Personal key only | Not bundled; install it on the service or execution machine PATH | The seven agent CLIs after Claude Code keep their model and MCP configuration in a private home directory per run, so they always use the responsible user's own key and Base URL from personal settings, even on a connected execution machine. When rolling them out to a team, each member configures their own credentials. First-use installs need npm or provider access; [native deployments](docs/deployment.md#workers-and-runners) need the CLI for the executor you choose. - **GitHub is optional.** All built-in generic SOPs run without a repository: product SOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs. - **Delivering to a repository.** Choose **Connect GitHub** in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project SOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR. - **Sandboxes.** In the default Compose installation, SOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles stil

name: openworker
readme_content:
OpenWorker

A Desktop App for everyday work.
A Harness SDK to power your AI ideas.

openworker.com · Desktop App · Harness SDK · Issues

Use the **OpenWorker Desktop App** to research, write, review code, and carry out tasks across the tools you already use. Or build your own agentic desktop and web apps with the **OpenWorker Harness SDK**. Bring your choice of cloud or local models. Set permissions for your agents and decide which actions need your approval. > This README mainly covers the **OpenWorker Desktop App**. For SDK setup, examples and architecture, see the [**OpenWorker Harness SDK README**](harness/README.md). ## Use the OpenWorker Desktop App An AI coworker for your everyday work. Go from a request to a prepared brief, an organized folder, or a reviewed pull request. It runs on your machine. Bring your own model key or run locally with Ollama, and choose which integrations it can access. Commands can run inside an [NVIDIA OpenShell](docs/openshell.md) sandbox. See [Governed by design](#governed-by-design) for its approval and safety controls. [![How the OpenWorker Desktop App works](docs/assets/how-it-works.png)](https://openworker.com) [⬇ macOS (Apple Silicon)](https://download.openworker.com/mac) macOS 12+ · signed & notarized · auto-updates [⬇ Windows 10/11 (x64)](https://download.openworker.com/windows) builds are not yet code-signed, so SmartScreen will warn; signing is in progress Open the app, add a model key (or point it at Ollama), and ask for something real. The OpenWorker Desktop App is in open beta and supports automatic updates. [Issues](https://github.com/andrewyng/openworker/issues) welcome as we polish rough edges. ## Build agentic apps using OpenWorker Harness SDK Bring agentic capabilities to your own desktop app, web app or local utility. Build the product experience while OpenWorker handles the agent loop, tool calls, approvals, streaming and durable sessions. Use the TypeScript SDK from npm, or embed the Rust engine in your application. Start with one agent. Add sub-agents, teams, OpenShell sandboxing and observability as your application grows. ```sh npm install @openworkerai/harness-sdk ``` [**Explore the Harness SDK →**](harness/README.md) · [Desktop guide](docs/harness/guides/desktop.md) · [Web guide](docs/harness/guides/server.md) · [Build with Codex or Claude Code](skills/README.md) The rest of this README focuses on the OpenWorker Desktop App. For SDK documentation, continue with the [Harness SDK README](harness/README.md). ## What you can do with the Desktop App | Your work | How OpenWorker helps | |---|---| | **Research and create** | Turn notes, files and research into briefs, documents, spreadsheets and reports. | | **Review security risks** | Scan code and dependencies, review cloud configuration, and investigate incidents. Proposed code fixes are re-scanned and reviewed before approval. | | **Work across your tools** | Bring together GitHub, Slack, email, calendars and other connected apps. Add tools through MCP. | | **Delegate from Slack** | Mention `@OpenWorker`; the task runs on your desktop and the reply returns to the thread. | | **Automate recurring work** | Schedule morning briefs, weekly reports and other repeatable tasks, with transcripts to review. | | **Choose your model** | Connect a cloud provider or use a local model through Ollama and other compatible servers. | | **Control agent actions** | Review approvals, inspect recorded actions, and isolate supported commands with OpenShell or platform sandboxing. | Specialist coworkers come with tools and instructions for a particular job. Security coworkers ship first. ## Try your first task Start with a folder of meeting notes. No connected apps are needed for this example. 1. **Choose a model.** Open **Settings → Models & Keys** and connect a provider or local model. 2. **Choose your working folder.** Give the session access to a folder containing a few text or Markdown notes. 3. **Ask for a brief.** Paste the request below, follow the tool activity, and review any approval requests before continuing. > Read the meeting notes in this folder. Create a one-page brief with the key decisions, open questions and next steps. Save it as `brief.md`. Leave the original notes unchanged and ask before writing the brief. ![Example workflow: meeting notes become a brief after you review the proposed write](docs/assets/first-task.svg) Open `brief.md` in the working folder and review it. Continue in the same session: “Make the next steps more specific, and flag anything without an owner.” ## Governed by design The Desktop App combines approvals, recorded tool activity and optional sandboxing. You can review proposed actions and decide how much autonomy to allow.
How approvals, audit trails and sandboxing work Governance is the architecture, not a plugin - the agent can't grant itself new permissions, and no prompt can talk it past a gate. Four tiers, all in this repo: 1. **Hard floors.** A set of dangerous and irreversible operations is human-only, always. No mode - including full auto-approve - lowers these floors; they always escalate to you. 2. **A ladder of earned autonomy.** Actions are approval-gated by default. One-off approvals can graduate into standing rules, then into config allowlists - each step explicit, visible, and revocable. In auto-approve mode a reviewer model lets routine actions through and escalates anything it isn't sure about to you; repeated denials trip a circuit breaker that pauses the reviewer and hands control back. Reviewer verdicts are judgments, not guarantees - the floors and the audit trail are what backstop them. 3. **An audit trail that answers "who did this, and why?"** Every tool call is recorded with its approval provenance - auto-approved, user-approved, or denied, with the reviewer's reasoning attached - and persisted with the conversation. 4. **A sandbox for what the agent runs.** A session's commands and file tools can run inside an [NVIDIA OpenShell](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell) sandbox — one Linux container per agent that holds the session's folders and nothing else: no keys, no other files, and only an allow list of network hosts. The agent loop, the model keys and the connectors stay outside the wall, so a prompt injection that reaches a command lands in a box that holds nothing. On a Mac the same protection is available with nothing to install, through the sandbox built into macOS; on Windows, through a hidden local account that cannot see your profile. See [docs/openshell.md](docs/openshell.md), [docs/macos-sandbox.md](docs/macos-sandbox.md) and [docs/windows-sandbox.md](docs/windows-sandbox.md). Unattended runs never self-approve: their asks park in an inbox until a human answers. Found a vulnerability? See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
## Bring your own model Connect OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenRouter and other providers, or use a local model through Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp or vLLM. Choose and switch models in **Settings → Models & Keys**. See [Desktop App model setup](docs/desktop-models.md) for provider options, account connections and custom endpoints. SDK developers can use the separate [models and credentials guide](docs/harness/guides/providers.md). ## Desktop App privacy The OpenWorker Desktop App is local-first. Everything lives on your machine: the agent loop, your conversations, connector tokens, and model keys - all in the app's local secret store. The only cloud piece is a small service that brokers OAuth handshakes for connectors. You can always use the App without signing-in - use the connectors via manually-created credentials/API-keys. ## Documentation | Start here | What you’ll find | |---|---| | [Desktop App model setup](docs/desktop-models.md) | Cloud providers, OpenRouter accounts and custom endpoints. | | [Local models](docs/local-servers.md) | Connect models running on your own hardware. | | [Approvals and safety](#governed-by-design) | How the Desktop App handles permissions and records actions. | | [NVIDIA OpenShell](docs/openshell.md) | Set up sandboxed command and file execution for the Desktop App. | | [Harness SDK](harness/README.md) | SDK installation, architecture and examples. | | [Build a desktop app](docs/harness/guides/desktop.md) · [Build a web app](docs/harness/guides/server.md) | Learn the SDK through working applications. | | [App-building skill](skills/README.md) | Build with Codex or Claude Code. | | [SDK troubleshooting](docs/harness/guides/troubleshooting.md) | Diagnose SDK setup and runtime problems. | ## Run the Desktop App from source
Development setup and architecture The Desktop App uses a Python agent engine. The Harness SDK provides a separate Rust engine for applications you build. Under the hood: ```text ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ OpenWorker Desktop App │ native shell + GUI ├────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ local agent server (Python) │ engine · tools · connectors - built on aisuite ├───────────────┬────────────────┬───────────────┤ │ your files │ your tools │ your model │ everything runs with your keys, │ & terminal │ 25+ connectors │ any provider │ on your machine └───────────────┴────────────────┴───────────────┘ ``` Prerequisites: Python 3.10+, Node 20+, and (for the desktop shell) the Rust toolchain via [rustup](https://rustup.rs/). ```shell git clone https://github.com/andrewyng/openworker cd openworker # 1. One-time bootstrap - creates the Python venv at .venv # (on Windows, run from Git Bash or WSL) bash packaging/setup_dev_env.sh # 2. Start the local agent server .venv/bin/python -m coworker.server.run --cwd ~/some/project --port 8765 # (Windows: .venv\Scripts\python -m coworker.server.run ...) # 3. In a second terminal, start the UI cd surfaces/gui npm install npm run dev # browser UI on the Vite dev port ``` The standalone server creates a per-launch token at `/sidecar-8765.token`; Vite reads that user-only file when it starts. For direct API calls, send its value in the `X-OpenWorker-Token` header. The desktop app uses an in-memory launch token instead and never writes it to disk. To run the full desktop app instead of the browser UI, replace step 3 with `npm run tauri dev` (from `surfaces/gui/`) - the Tauri shell launches the window and supervises the server itself. Tests: `.venv/bin/pytest` (server), `npm test` and `npm run e2e` in `surfaces/gui` (GUI unit + hermetic end-to-end). Desktop bundles are built with `packaging/build_dmg.sh` / `packaging/build_windows.ps1`.
## Repository layout | Directory | What's in it | |---|---| | `coworker/` | Python backend - agent engine, model providers, connectors, MCP client, memory, automations | | `harness/` | Rust agent runtime, Rust/TypeScript SDKs, service and SDK examples | | `surfaces/gui/`
manifest_content:
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "openworker"
version = "0.3.4"
description = "OpenWorker — an open-source AI coworker you govern. The headless runtime and CLI."
readme = "README.md"
license = { text = "MIT" }
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
    "openai>=1.0",
    "anthropic>=0.40",  # native Claude Messages API provider
    "google-genai>=1.0",  # native Gemini provider
    "google-auth>=2.23",  # Vertex credentials (service account / ADC / MaaS bearer)
    "textual>=1.0",
    "fastapi>=0.110",
    "uvicorn[standard]>=0.27",
    # aisuite (tool metadata, toolkits, tracing). 0.2.0 is the first PyPI release with those modules.
    "aisuite>=0.2.0",
    "docstring_parser",
    "pyyaml>=6",  # persona manifest frontmatter (YAML)
    "pydantic>=2",
    "mcp>=1.28.1,<2",  # MCP client (stdio + streamable-http); floor >=1.28.1 avoids PYSEC-2026-3481/3482/3483 (fixed in 1.27.2/1.28.1); <2 since 2.0.0 removed streamablehttp_client
    "httpx>=0.27",  # sync outbound senders for messaging connectors (send_message tool)
    "websockets>=13",  # managed Slack relay client transport (relay_client.py) + remote-home joiner
    "cryptography>=42",  # ed25519 machine identity for remote homes (already transitive via google-auth)
    "ddgs>=9",  # keyless default web-search provider (DuckDuckGo); Tavily/Brave use httpx
    "croniter>=2",  # cron next-fire math for the automation scheduler
    # PDF attachments for models without native PDF support (pdf_support.py):
    # pypdf = pure-python text extraction; pypdfium2 = page rasterization (BSD pdfium,
    # ships its own libpdfium — NOT PyMuPDF, whose AGPL license can't ride in the DMG).
    "pypdf>=5",
    "pypdfium2>=4",
    # IANA tz database for zoneinfo. Windows ships no system tz db, so without this every
    # named schedule timezone (UTC, Asia/Kolkata, …) silently falls back to local time.
    "tzdata; sys_platform == 'win32'",
    # tomllib landed in the 3.11 stdlib; on the 3.10 floor config.py falls back to tomli.
    "tomli>=2; python_version < '3.11'",
]

[project.urls]
Homepage = "https://openworker.com"
Source = "https://github.com/andrewyng/openworker"

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "pytest-asyncio", "pytest-cov>=5", "httpx", "httpx2"]
# Inbound messaging listeners (outbound send_message needs only httpx, already a core dep).
# aiohttp is slack-bolt's Socket Mode transport at runtime (and the FakeSlack test harness
# drives the real handler) — declare it so CI installs it, not just transitively.
messaging = ["python-telegram-bot>=21", "slack-bolt>=1.18", "aiohttp>=3.9"]
# Interactive Cowork browser automation.
browser = ["playwright>=1.44"]
# AWS Bedrock provider (lazy-imported; desktop builds bundle it, pip users opt in).
bedrock = ["boto3>=1.34"]
# OpenShell sandbox provider: the runner's stream is a gRPC call to the OpenShell gateway.
openshell = ["grpcio>=1.60"]

# One command on the path. The server, the connectors tool, the acceptor and the team
# board stay runnable as modules (`python -m coworker.server.run`, …) for development.
[project.scripts]
openworker = "coworker.cli:main"

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["."]
include = ["coworker*"]

[tool.setuptools.package-data]
coworker = [
    "personas/builtin/*.md",
    "personas/builtin/*/manifest.md",
    "personas/builtin/*/skills/*/SKILL.md",
    "headless/*.yaml",
    "observability/*.yaml",
    "providers/*.json",
]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
# The reviewer-eval tests import from the repo-root scripts/ package; the pytest
# console script (CI) does not put the root on sys.path the way `python -m pytest` does.
pythonpath = ["."]
asyncio_mode = "auto"

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["coworker"]
branch = true
omit = [
    "*/tests/*",
    "*/__pycache__/*",
    "*/migrations/*",
]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
skip_covered = false
precision = 1
# Ratchet floor — only goes up, never down.
# Run `pytest tests --cov=coworker --cov-report=term-missing` to see current coverage.
fail_under = 0
exclude_lines = [
    "pragma: no cover",
    "def __repr__",
    "raise NotImplementedError",
    "if TYPE_CHECKING:",
    "if __name__ == .__main__.:",
]

name: headroom
description: Compress tool outputs, logs, files, and RAG chunks before they reach the LLM. 20% fewer tokens for coding agents, 60-95% fewer tokens for JSON, same answers. Library, proxy, MCP server.
readme_content:
Quickstart · Headroom for Teams · Install · Proof · Agents · Docs · Discord · llms.txt

AI agents / LLMs: read /llms.txt here, or fetch the live index · full docs blob.
**Headroom** (`headroom-ai` on PyPI and npm) compresses everything your AI agent reads — tool outputs, logs, RAG chunks, files, and conversation history — before it reaches the LLM. Same answers, fewer input tokens. Measured: 21–57% fewer input tokens on four agent scenarios, 90%+ on repeated JSON arrays and log lines, little on prose ([Proof](#proof-measured-token-savings)). Compression runs on your machine; no prompt or file content is sent anywhere to be compressed. ## Start here **My app calls an LLM** (Python, LangChain, LiteLLM, Agno, Strands): ```bash pip install headroom-ai ``` ```python from headroom import compress result = compress(messages, model="gpt-4o") # OpenAI or Anthropic message dicts client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o", messages=result.messages) ``` No API key, no model download, in-process. Set `HEADROOM_OFFLINE=1` for a zero-network run. Tool and assistant messages are compressed; user messages are left alone unless you pass `compress_user_messages=True`. [FastAPI example](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/fastapi) · [API reference](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/api-reference). TypeScript apps: `npm install headroom-ai` plus the proxy (`pip install "headroom-ai[proxy]"`, `headroom proxy --port 8787`); the npm SDK sends messages to it. [TypeScript quickstart](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/quickstart) **I run coding agents** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode, Aider): ```bash uv tool install --python 3.13 "headroom-ai[all]" headroom wrap claude ``` Zero code changes. [Agent compatibility](#agent-compatibility) · [Proxy](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/proxy)


10,144 → 1,260 tokens. The same FATAL found.
## What it does - **Library** — `compress(messages)` in Python or TypeScript, inline in any app. - **Proxy** — `headroom proxy --port 8787`, zero code changes, any language. - **Agent wrap** — `headroom wrap claude|codex|grok|copilot|cursor|aider|opencode|cline|continue|goose|openhands|openclaw|vibe|omp|droid|zcode` in one command; undo with `headroom unwrap `. - **MCP server** — `headroom_compress`, `headroom_retrieve`, `headroom_stats` for any MCP client. - **Cross-agent memory** — one shared store across Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok, with automatic dedup. - **`headroom learn`** — mines failed sessions and writes corrections to `CLAUDE.local.md` (default, gitignored), `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md` or `GROK.md`. - **Output token reduction** — trims what the model *writes back*, not only what you send. See [below](#output-token-reduction). - **Reversible (CCR)** — originals are cached locally and retrieved on demand. ## How it works ``` Your agent / app (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, LangChain, Agno, Strands, your own code…) │ prompts · tool outputs · logs · RAG results · files ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Headroom (runs locally — your data stays here) │ │ ──────────────────────────────────────────────── │ │ CacheAligner → ContentRouter → CCR │ │ ├─ SmartCrusher (JSON) │ │ ├─ CodeCompressor (AST) │ │ └─ Kompress-v2-base (text, HF) │ │ │ │ Cross-agent memory · headroom learn · MCP │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ compressed prompt + retrieval tool ▼ LLM provider (Anthropic · OpenAI · Bedrock · …) ``` - **ContentRouter** detects the content type and selects a compressor for it. - **SmartCrusher / CodeCompressor / Kompress-v2-base** handle JSON, source code and prose respectively. - **CacheAligner** flags volatile content that would bust a provider KV-cache prefix. It never rewrites prompts. - **CCR** stores originals locally so the model can call `headroom_retrieve` when it needs the full text. → [Architecture](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/architecture) · [CCR](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/ccr) · [Kompress-v2-base model card](https://huggingface.co/chopratejas/kompress-v2-base) ## Get started (60 seconds) ```bash # 1 — Install uv tool install --python 3.13 "headroom-ai[all]" # CLI in a self-contained env pip install "headroom-ai[all]" # Python — ships the `headroom` CLI npm install headroom-ai # TypeScript SDK only — no CLI # 2 — Pick a mode headroom deploy # turnkey local deployment + agent config headroom wrap claude # wrap a coding agent headroom proxy --port 8787 # drop-in proxy, zero code changes # or: from headroom import compress # inline library # 3 — Check it and watch the savings headroom doctor # health check — confirms routing works headroom perf headroom dashboard # live savings (proxy must be running) ``` ### Reduce input tokens in your own app ```python from headroom import compress from openai import OpenAI messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Analyze these results"}] result = compress(messages, model="gpt-4o") client = OpenAI() response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o", messages=result.messages) print(f"Saved {result.tokens_saved} tokens ({result.compression_ratio:.0%})") ``` Launch a wrapped agent session each time, so the setup runs. `headroom wrap` starts a local proxy and launches the agent configured to route through Headroom. Add `--code-memory serena` to also install **[Serena](https://github.com/oraios/serena)** for semantic code navigation (off by default). For Claude Code, Serena is registered for the wrapped project only (as a `local`-scope MCP server in `~/.claude.json`); use `--code-memory-scope user` to make it available in every project. `headroom unwrap` removes either registration. `headroom wrap ...` is session-scoped: its proxy exits with the wrapped agent. For a proxy that survives reboots, use the turnkey `headroom deploy` command. Use `headroom install apply` when you need to choose a specific persistent service, scheduled task, Docker runtime, scope, or provider target; see the [persistent installs guide](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/persistent-installs). The `headroom` CLI ships only in the PyPI package. The npm `headroom-ai` package is the TypeScript SDK — a library you import (`import { compress } from 'headroom-ai'`) — and provides no `headroom` command. ## Proof: measured token savings Four scenarios built from real MCP server output formats, measured with the provider tokenizer and the shipped `compress()` at its default configuration. Seeded and offline, so you get the same numbers we did: ```bash uv run python benchmarks/index_proof_table.py --seed 20260902 ``` | Scenario | Before | After | Saved | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Code search (100 results) | 17,199 | 13,597 | **21%** | | SRE incident debugging | 55,957 | 24,340 | **57%** | | Codebase exploration | 58,801 | 33,895 | **42%** | | GitHub issue triage | 46,067 | 32,429 | **30%** | Savings scale with how repetitive the payload is. Repeated JSON arrays and log lines clear 90% in `benchmarks/bench_latency.py`; prose and already-dense output compress very little. Run `headroom savings` against your own traffic for the number that applies to you. Compression costs **well under a millisecond** — 0.21 ms p50 on a 10K-token JSON search result, 1.4 ms at 100K tokens — so it does not show up in agent latency. **Accuracy.** `python -m headroom.evals suite --tier 1`: | Benchmark | Category | N | Baseline | Headroom | Delta | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---| | GSM8K | Math | 100 | 0.870 | 0.870 | ±0.000 | | TruthfulQA | Factual | 100 | 0.530 | 0.560 | +0.030 | | SQuAD v2 | QA | 100 | — | 97% | at 19% compression | | BFCL | Tools | 100 | — | 97% | at 32% compression | At N=100 a delta of ±0.03 falls inside the confidence interval, so TruthfulQA shows no detectable difference rather than an improvement. [Methodology →](https://docs.headroomlabs.ai/docs/benchmarks) ## Output token reduction Everything above shrinks the prompt you **send**. You also pay for every token the model **writes back**, and on Opus-class models output costs 5× input. Much of that output is ceremony: "Great, let me…" preambles, code re-printed straight back at you, and deep reasoning spent on routine steps like reading a file. Headroom trims it from the proxy, with no change to your code: - **Verbosity steering** appends a short "be terse, don't restate context" note to the *end* of the system prompt, so your prompt cache still hits. It applies to Anthropic `/v1/messages` and to OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses`, with the same `output_shaper:*` labels on all paths. ```bash export HEADROOM_

dependencies = [

    "pydantic>=2.0.0",            # Config and data models
    # Model registry, pricing and non-core providers; all lazily imported and
    # ImportError-guarded. 1.96.2 is the first litellm with prebuilt wheels for
    # Python 3.11-3.14 on Linux, macOS and Windows: older releases either reject
    # Python 3.14 (GH #956) or fall back to a Rust source build.
    "litellm>=1.96.2,<2.0",
    "click>=8.5.0",               # CLI framework; PYSEC-2026-2132 fix (command injection in click.edit())
    "rich>=13.0.0",               # Rich terminal output
    "opentelemetry-api>=1.45.2",  # CVE-2026-114603 tracestate parsing; CVE-2026-126360 traceparent ReDoS

    "hf-xet>=1.6.0; platform_machine == 'AMD64' or platform_machine == 'aarch64' or platform_machine == 'amd64' or platform_machine == 'arm64' or platform_machine == 'x86_64'",

    # with it pip takes litellm 1.103.7 (uv.lock has 1.101.0). Declared here so

    "filelock>=4.2.1",
]

proxy = [
